<PubmedArticle><MedlineCitation Status="MEDLINE" Owner="NLM" IndexingMethod="Manual"><PMID Version="1">26389628</PMID><DateCompleted><Year>2016</Year><Month>12</Month><Day>13</Day></DateCompleted><DateRevised><Year>2024</Year><Month>03</Month><Day>24</Day></DateRevised><Article PubModel="Print-Electronic"><Journal><ISSN IssnType="Electronic">1939-1285</ISSN><JournalIssue CitedMedium="Internet"><Volume>42</Volume><Issue>3</Issue><PubDate><Year>2016</Year><Month>Mar</Month></PubDate></JournalIssue><Title>Journal of experimental psychology. Learning, memory, and cognition</Title><ISOAbbreviation>J Exp Psychol Learn Mem Cogn</ISOAbbreviation></Journal><ArticleTitle>Retrieval-induced versus context-induced forgetting: Does retrieval-induced forgetting depend on context shifts?</ArticleTitle><Pagination><StartPage>366</StartPage><EndPage>378</EndPage><MedlinePgn>366-78</MedlinePgn></Pagination><ELocationID EIdType="doi" ValidYN="Y">10.1037/xlm0000171</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText>Retrieval-induced forgetting (RIF) is the observation that retrieval of target information causes forgetting of related nontarget information. A number of accounts of this phenomenon have been proposed, including a context-shift-based account (Jonker, Seli, &amp; Macleod, 2013). This account proposes that RIF occurs as a result of the context shift from study to retrieval practice, provided there is little context shift between retrieval practice and test phases. We tested both claims put forth by this context account. In Experiment 1, we degraded the context shift between study and retrieval practice by implementing a generative study condition that was highly similar to retrieval practice. We observed no degradation of RIF for these generated exemplars relative to a conventional study control. In Experiment 2, we conceptually replicated the finding of RIF following generative study, and tested whether context differences between each of the three phases affected the size of RIF. Our findings were again contrary to the predictions of the context account. Conjointly, the 2 experiments refute arguments about the potential inadequacy of our context shifts that could be used to explain either result alone. Overall, our results are most consistent with an inhibitory account of RIF (e.g., Anderson, 2003).</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>(c) 2016 APA, all rights
